tier_reason: PERFORMANCE.md states Go 1.17, Intel Core i7-10510U with turbo disabled, and native (AVX2 assembly) versus purego builds. The stdlib head-to-heads are reproducible from in-repo benchmark code: primitives/ed25519/ed25519_test.go (BenchmarkSigning and BenchmarkVerification, with voi and stdlib sub-benchmarks), primitives/ed25519/batch_verify_test.go and primitives/x25519/x25519_test.go (voi vs x/crypto). Go's gc compiler has no optimisation flags beyond the build tag, so tier A holds.

corrections.baseline: Go standard library crypto/ed25519 and golang.org/x/crypto/curve25519 (X25519) for single operations; ed25519consensus (hdevalence) for batch verification, since stdlib has no batch verify; Cloudflare CIRCL also benchmarked
corrections.claimed_speedup: Native (AVX2) build, Go 1.17, i7-10510U. Ed25519 Verify: 125us (stdlib) to 75us, about 1.67x (derived from page data). Sign: 52.7us to 27.5us, about 1.92x (derived from page data). NewKeyFromSeed: 42.8us to 24.3us. X25519 ScalarBaseMult: 107us (x/crypto) to 24us, about 4.5x (derived from page data). X25519 ScalarMult shows no gain (107us vs 106us), and CIRCL is faster there at 65us. Batch verification is measured against ed25519consensus, not stdlib: VerifyBatch_1024 goes from 61.8ms to 31.7ms, about 1.95x (derived from page data), and to 24.0ms with precomputed expanded public keys. With the purego build (no assembly), Verify goes from 181us to 121us and Sign from 73.3us to 50.9us.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 79 stars; oasis-core's go.mod pins curve25519-voi and replaces golang.org/x/crypto/ed25519 and x/crypto/curve25519 with it
corrections.caveats: The batch-verify baseline is ed25519consensus, not Go stdlib, which has no batch verification. X25519 variable-base ScalarMult is no faster than x/crypto, and CIRCL (which uses BMI2) beats it. The benchmark harness for the CIRCL and ed25519consensus comparisons is not in the repo; only the stdlib and x/crypto comparisons are. All numbers come from a single 2021-era laptop CPU on Go 1.17. There is no comparison with OpenSSL or libsodium.

notes: This is a downgrade for a misattributed claim, not for the tier (it stays A). The record credited the 61.8ms to 31.7ms VerifyBatch_1024 win to stdlib, but that column is ed25519consensus. The record's /blob/main/ benchmark URL returns 404 because the default branch is master. The last commit on master is 2025-11-14, about 10 months ago, so the project is active, not stale.

tier_reason: The README says the Secp256k1 FFI backend 'provides performance faster than the native Rust implementation k256 library by ~30% on verification'. It gives no methodology, hardware or benchmark. fastcrypto/benches/crypto.rs has no k256 comparison, so this is first-party and tier C.

corrections.caveats: The ~30% figure is a first-party README claim with no stated methodology, hardware or reproducible benchmark; the repo's benches do not compare against k256. The speed comes entirely from bitcoin-core/libsecp256k1, reached through the rust-secp256k1 crate (Cargo.toml: rust_secp256k1 = secp256k1 0.27.0); fastcrypto adds only a wrapper.

notes: The claim in the record matches the README, and the metadata is correct (Apache-2.0, 311 stars, last commit 2026-09-25). The win belongs to https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1, which is already on the known list and verified at tier A in wave 7. The eth.zig entry, which vendors the same library, was already marked duplicate in decisions.json on the same grounds. If the orchestrator would rather keep a Rust-ecosystem entry, confirm it at tier C.

tier_reason: The go-libp2p CHANGELOG (v0.25.0, 'Removal of OpenSSL') makes only a qualitative claim, with no numbers. The linked benchmarks in issue #1952 and PR #1686 show Ed25519 at parity, and even those 'OpenSSL' columns ran Go code (see notes), so no non-RSA measurement against OpenSSL exists.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The CHANGELOG asserts, without numbers, that 'The Go standard library is faster than OpenSSL for all key types that are not RSA'. It also says RSA verify in Go stdlib is about as fast as Ed25519 in Go stdlib and 'even faster in OpenSSL', and that RSA signing is slower in Go stdlib. The linked benchmarks show Ed25519 sign and verify at parity: verify at 1B is 76.2us Go vs 82.3us for the '-tags openssl' build in issue #1952, and 55.7us vs 55.1us in the PR #1686 comment. There are no ECDSA numbers. For RSA, OpenSSL was faster: verify 80.5us Go vs 14.0us OpenSSL, and sign 1983us vs 680us (issue #1686 comment 1347546446).
corrections.caveats: go-libp2p's openssl build tag only routed RSA keys through OpenSSL (core/crypto/key_openssl.go and openssl_common.go at v0.24.2). Ed25519, ECDSA and secp256k1 always used Go code, so the Ed25519 'OpenSSL' benchmark columns measure the same Go code. Where OpenSSL was actually measured (RSA), Go stdlib was 3-7x slower.

notes: The record's claim cannot be supported. go-libp2p never used OpenSSL for non-RSA keys, so no head-to-head against OpenSSL for Ed25519 or ECDSA exists anywhere in these sources, and the only real OpenSSL comparison (RSA) shows Go stdlib slower. The record also misparaphrased the RSA line: OpenSSL RSA verify is faster, not on par. If kept, it should sit at tier D with the corrected claim above.
